title: Influence of intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) on xerostomia, salivary pH, and quality of life in patients with tumors of the oral cavity and pharynx (pre- and post-IMRT).
summary:
IMRT is a specialized form of radiotherapy that aims to treat tumors as precisely as possible while sparing surrounding healthy tissue, especially sensitive organs. This can help reduce side effects and improve patients’ quality of life.

Studies show that IMRT can particularly reduce xerostomia as a long-term side effect. This is especially true for techniques that specifically spare the parotid glands.

In oropharyngeal carcinoma, a cancer located in the throat area, the long-term side effects of radiotherapy are not always predictable. This is partly due to the fact that the condition includes a wide range of tumor types – for example, in the oral cavity, the pharynx, the hypopharynx, the nasopharynx, and the larynx.

The situation is particularly challenging in oral cavity carcinomas, as the submandibular glands are often located directly adjacent to the tumor or affected lymph nodes. As a result, they often cannot be spared, which increases the risk of severe xerostomia after treatment.

Dry mouth (xerostomia) can generally be measured using quality-of-life questionnaires or saliva tests. In saliva testing, either natural (unstimulated) saliva flow is measured over a certain period, or salivation is stimulated, for example using paraffin film.

In addition to xerostomia, radiotherapy can also affect the pH value of saliva. Normally, saliva has a pH of about 6.8. After radiation, it can drop below 5. This reduces the protective buffering function of saliva and increases the risk of radiation-induced dental caries.

Salivary pH is measured using a pH meter or special pH test strips. Studies show that the pH value reaches its lowest point approximately six weeks after radiation therapy. In many cases, it remains below the baseline level for years after treatment.

interventions.name: In patients receiving radiotherapy in the head and neck region, salivary flow rate, salivary pH, and questionnaires (oral health, salivary flow rate) are measured at T0, T1, T2, and T3.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with oropharyngeal tumors (ICD C00–C10, C14) undergoing IMRT.
Exclusion criteria:
Lack of patient consent; Patients with dementia or other cognitive impairments who are unable to provide informed consent; Patients who decline participation in the study for other reasons
